questions.question: Which HTTP method should be used to create a new resource in a RESTful API?

options.text: GET - retrieves or creates resources as needed
POST - creates new resources
PUT - creates or updates resources
PATCH - creates resources with partial data

questions.explanation: POST creates new resources. GET retrieves (and must be safe/idempotent), PUT replaces entirely (idempotent), PATCH partially updates. POST to a collection endpoint (e.g., POST /users) creates a new resource with server-assigned ID. While PUT can create if you know the ID upfront (PUT /users/123), POST is the standard for creation when the server assigns identifiers. Stripe's API uses POST /v1/customers to create customers.

questions.question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH in REST?

options.text: PUT is for creating; PATCH is for updating existing resources
PUT replaces the entire resource; PATCH updates specific fields
PUT is idempotent; PATCH is not idempotent
PUT requires authentication; PATCH does not

questions.explanation: PUT replaces the entire resource (must send complete representation). PATCH applies partial modifications (send only changed fields). Using PUT for partial updates can accidentally null omitted fields—a common bug. GitHub's API uses PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo} to update repository settings without replacing the entire resource. Both can be idempotent if implemented correctly; the difference is complete vs. partial replacement.

questions.question: Which REST endpoint design follows best practices for getting a specific user?

options.text: GET /getUser?id=123
GET /users/123
POST /users/get with {"id": 123} body
GET /api/v1/user/fetch/123

questions.explanation: RESTful URLs use nouns (resources) not verbs. /users/123 identifies the resource; the HTTP method (GET) specifies the action. Query parameters are for filtering collections, not resource identification. Twitter, GitHub, and Stripe all follow this pattern: GET /users/{id}, GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}, GET /v1/customers/{id}. Verbs in URLs (getUser, fetch) indicate RPC-style design, not REST.

questions.question: Which HTTP status codes indicate client errors? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: 400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error

questions.explanation: 4xx codes are client errors: 400 (malformed request syntax), 401 (authentication required), 404 (resource doesn't exist). 500 is a server error—the server failed to fulfill a valid request. The distinction matters for retry logic: 4xx errors won't succeed on retry (fix the request), while 5xx might (transient server issue). Stripe returns detailed error codes within 4xx responses to help developers fix issues.

questions.question: An API returns 201 Created. What should the response include?

options.text: Nothing - the status code alone is sufficient
Location header with the new resource's URL
Redirect instruction to the login page
Error details for client-side validation

questions.explanation: 201 Created should include a Location header pointing to the newly created resource (e.g., Location: /users/456). The response body often includes the created resource representation, saving a subsequent GET request. AWS API Gateway, GitHub, and most well-designed APIs follow this pattern. This enables clients to immediately access or reference the new resource without parsing response bodies.

questions.question: What does HATEOAS stand for and what does it enable?

options.text: HTTP Authentication Token Exchange - enables secure token-based auth
Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State - enables API discoverability
High Availability Through Elastic Auto Scaling - enables dynamic scaling
Hypertext Application Transfer Over Secure Sockets - enables encrypted communication

questions.explanation: HATEOAS means responses include links to related actions/resources, allowing clients to navigate the API dynamically without hardcoding URLs. It's the highest level of REST maturity (Richardson Maturity Model Level 3). PayPal's API exemplifies this: a payment response includes links to capture, void, or refund. While powerful, many APIs skip HATEOAS for simplicity—it adds complexity but enables truly evolvable APIs.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to version a REST API?

options.text: Only URL path versioning (/v1/users) is RESTful
Only header versioning (Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json) is RESTful
Multiple approaches exist; URL path and header versioning are both common
REST APIs should never be versioned - use feature flags instead

questions.explanation: Both URL versioning (/v1/) and header versioning are valid approaches with tradeoffs. URL is more visible, cacheable, and easier to test (Stripe uses /v1/). Headers are more 'pure' REST but harder to test in browsers (GitHub uses Accept headers). Twilio uses date-based versioning. The key is consistency and clear deprecation policies, not which method you choose.

questions.question: A REST API needs to return a filtered list of users. Which approach is most RESTful?

options.text: POST /users/filter with filter criteria in request body
GET /users?status=active&role=admin
GET /filterUsers/active/admin
GET /users/search with criteria in custom headers

questions.explanation: GET with query parameters is RESTful for filtering collections—it's cacheable and bookmarkable. POST for filtering violates REST semantics (GET for retrieval, POST for creation). Embedding filters in URL path conflates filtering with resource identification. GitHub uses GET /repos?type=public&sort=updated. Query parameters are designed for filtering, sorting, and pagination.

questions.question: True or False: A RESTful API must use JSON for request and response bodies.

options.text: True - JSON is the REST standard
False - REST is format-agnostic

questions.explanation: REST is format-agnostic. While JSON is most common today, REST APIs can use XML, YAML, Protocol Buffers, or other formats. Content-Type and Accept headers negotiate the format. AWS APIs support both JSON and XML. The original REST dissertation by Roy Fielding doesn't mention JSON at all—it predates JSON's popularity. REST is about architectural constraints, not data formats.

questions.question: Which HTTP methods are idempotent? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: GET
POST
PUT
DELETE

questions.explanation: Idempotent methods produce the same result regardless of how many times called. GET (read same data), PUT (replace with same data), DELETE (resource stays deleted) are idempotent. POST is not—each call may create a new resource. This matters for retry logic: safe to retry idempotent methods on network failure. Stripe uses idempotency keys with POST to make non-idempotent operations safe to retry.

questions.question: An API endpoint sometimes takes 30 seconds to process. What is the best approach?

options.text: Increase timeout and make client wait synchronously
Return 202 Accepted with a status URL for polling
Return partial results immediately and complete later
Split into multiple smaller synchronous calls

questions.explanation: 202 Accepted indicates the request is processing asynchronously. The response includes a URL to check status (polling) or a webhook for completion notification. This prevents timeouts and allows the client to continue other work. AWS uses this pattern for long-running operations like CloudFormation stack creation. GitHub uses it for repository imports. The pattern: POST returns 202 + status URL, GET on status URL returns progress or result.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the ETag header in REST APIs?

options.text: To encrypt the response payload
To enable conditional requests and caching
To identify the API version being used
To authenticate the client making the request

questions.explanation: ETag is a resource version identifier (like a hash of content). Clients use If-None-Match for caching (return 304 Not Modified if unchanged) or If-Match for optimistic concurrency (fail if resource changed since last read). GitHub uses ETags extensively—polling for notifications returns 304 if nothing changed, saving bandwidth. ETags prevent lost updates in concurrent editing scenarios.
